question: A patient on basal insulin glargine at bedtime has consistent fasting glucose readings of 160-180 mg/dL, but postprandial readings are 130-150 mg/dL. Which adjustment is most appropriate based on SMBG data?

answers.text: Add a rapid-acting insulin before each meal to correct postprandial hyperglycaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Postprandial readings of 130-150 mg/dL are near-target. The problem is fasting hyperglycaemia (160-180 mg/dL), which indicates the basal insulin dose needs upward titration, not the addition of mealtime insulin.

answers.text: Increase the bedtime glargine dose to reduce fasting hyperglycaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Consistently elevated fasting glucose with near-normal postprandial readings indicates inadequate basal insulin coverage overnight. The standard approach is to increase glargine by 2 units every 3 days until fasting target (80-130 mg/dL) is achieved.
Switching to NPH is a step backwards — NPH has unpredictable peak and higher hypoglycaemia risk. The issue is dose inadequacy, not the wrong insulin type.

answers.text: The SMBG pattern is acceptable — no adjustment needed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fasting glucose of 160-180 mg/dL is above the ADA target of 80-130 mg/dL. This pattern clearly indicates the need for basal insulin titration.

overallFeedback.feedback: SMBG pattern interpretation: high fasting = basal insulin inadequate; high postprandial = mealtime insulin needed. Here, fasting 160-180 with near-normal postprandial = increase basal glargine.
Well done — isolated fasting hyperglycaemia with good postprandial control indicates basal insulin underdosing. Titrate glargine upward.
